Then thou art mad thy selfe. Now thou talkest wildly. If it bee so, that may conclude I ha' lost 'em, And doe not understand my selfe. Prethee tell mee, thou art a peece of a Philosopher, And knowest the naturall causes. Why then acknowledge, I am mad, and I have done. But wherefore doe y'allow it, what's the cause? Ile tell thee then. And let thy judgement censure mee If I produce not able reasons— But of one? Did they not both affect mee, and I them With such equality of honour. And I to lose 'em both? faith speake but honestly; Is't not a wonder that I doe not rave And kill my selfe? how many have runne mad For one that never lov'd 'em? and shall I Bee so unmannerly not to lose my wits For two and two such creatures? twere a Solecisme In love: I prethee doe not flatter mee With an opinion that I have my reason; It cannot bee, it is against all sense, I should haue any; such an expectation Lost, is enough to make the genius Of all the world runne mad, and I will straight. To Bedlem, whether should I goe? I must not live in this community of fooles and wisemen. Here all are happy, there I sha'not meet With lovers that are fortunate, but with men Of my complexion, that looke twenty wayes At once, that sigh and curse, and sing mad Carols: If I can get to bee their Prince, Ile make A law it shall bee death to smile or kisse A woman. Nay, wee'le have An excellent well governd Common wealth, A delicate Eutopia, there shall be Lectures and publike readings shall put downe Gressams foundation for the liberall Arts, And make the Citizens bring their Shop-bookes hither To take fine notes, how to bee paid their debts, And yet trust none but younger brothers: then Wee will have penall Statutes against eating, Live all by the ayre of commendations. No idle man shall live within our State: Doe y' marke? they are the mouthes of the Republike: And therefore hee that has no other worke To prevent slothfulnesse, may imploy his time In picking strawes, there will be a great plenty. Here will wee live together, and bee mad Perpetually, wee wo'not bee recovered; For if at any time wee incline to bee Sober, and comming to our wits againe, The lash will whip us into new distempers And mad fugaries. I prethee pardon and instruct me better; I am not well. No, I am well againe. Vpon condition you will tell Aurelia Shee did not use me kindly. She did not use me kindly, nothing else, Farewell. Exit. I once beleev'd women were full of pitty, Of soft and gentle constitutions: But I have found 'em cruell: for Aurelia, One of the best of all her sex, doth owne A hard and tyrannous nature. Enter servant. I prethee let it be vndone, as I am. I gave to be taught Musicke? Ile hear't anon: I prethee goe — To Prison. Yes, and aske when are the Sessions. I would 'twere execution day to morrow. I would intreat the Surgeons to beg Some Woman for Anatomy, nothing else: I have heard their Lectures very much commended, And I'd be present when they read upon Her heart: for sure there is much difference Betweene a Woman and a Man, in that Same thing we call a heart, they doe not love As we doe; we are fooles, indeed we are, To dote so much upon 'em, and betray The glory of our creation, to serve A female pride; we were borne free, and had From the great Maker Royall priviledge, Most brave immunities: but since have made Tame forfeit of our Charter. Let me see't, It is the same, first read it, reach the chaire: Tis yet no Song, infuse a soule into it. Ha, tis not shee, doe I dreame still; Come hither, dost thou see nothing? Doe not abuse thy master, 'tis not possible Aurelia Will doe me so much honour; in my sleepe Me thought I parled with her, and my fancy Hath not yet lost her shape; Oh my Aurelia! Doe not mocke me ▪ Thou wo't bee cruell when I wake agen; And then I shall repent I dream't so sweetly. Let not the ground be hallowed with Such water, I have a heart to drinke this Balsome: Enough Aurelia, doe not make thy eyes Poore, to enrich thy bosome, where the drops Shew like a Carkanet of Pearle upon it, Thou hast enough restor'd mee. Tis sinne not to obey. It is to heaven thou goest. Convey mee swiftly thither. What blisse can bee deny'd, A man that followes such an Angell-guide? Exeunt. Gentle Neece, Misconster not my actions, 'tis my care Of thee, and to satisfie the duty I owe to my dead Brother, thy kinde parent: I thus restraine thee, thou art young, and canst not. Being so good thy selfe, suspect the world Hath any false men in't; I know there are Gallants, that study to undoe such Virgins As thou art, that will flatter and betray Thy fortunes to their riot, this unhappinesse I would prevent, and have new found a man, Into whose armes I may deliver up The wealth that I am trusted with. What successe? Good Master Yongrave: how doe you like this Gentleman. Doe what you please, I rellish not your ayre, Thats onely sweet to mee that profit brings, There is no musicke without golden strings. Sir, I must desire You would excuse me, I would goe with you, But that I have considered, 'twill be better That I should not appeare, since you intend To have it private, there will be lesse notice If I be absent, and it may be thought You by some tricke stole her away: D'yee marke? Then, sir, that opinion Will save our credit, and excuse the want Of ceremony, and the fruitlesse charge, Which is expected at her marriage: Is it not best? Y'are not wise, Eugenia, goe to the Church, and let me Salute you quickly happy bride and bridegroome: Away, I say. The Land's my own, you wrong your joyes to tarry, I would I had more Neeces thus to marry. Exit. Is not my Neece Eugenia here? Is't possible? is there no plot in this? I will tell you Sir, You doe remember Master Yongrave. Chris. unveiles. Ha, another Sweetheart; I am abus'd, hee is a very Knave; where is my Neece?
Hee's welcome: Pray what's your businesse? You come a wooing doe ye not? Heigho! Troth, if you be a good man, bee not tedious, I doe not love set speeches nor long praises, I hope y'ave made no verses o'my haire, Acrosticks o'my name, I hate them worse Than witchcraft, or the place I live in: if You be a sutor, put me out of my paine, Quickly I beseech you. My servant? what can you doe? I cannot helpe it, 'tis none of my fault. I cannot, Vnlesse I counterfeit, I have not smil'd These ten moneths; if a sigh will pleasure you, I can afford enough to breake your heart, And yet I live. Walke into the other roome, You'l find an alteration in the ayre, And thinke you come into a mist, which I Made all with my owne sighes, but I would not Infect you so; you seeme an honest Gentleman. 'Tis in the power Of one, that would be kinde to helpe me, but— You may love me too much, To undertake that taske. Oh yes, for though I should esteeme him deare, And call him my true friend, that in this storme Would lend a cord to save me, yet such is The misery of the imployment, he must not Love me too well that does it. I release these hasty Protestations. I will, athough Every syllable you speake, makes me suspect, You will repent this freedome. If you will doe A gratefull Office to me, in your person ▪ Give this paper to a Gentleman. gives him a letter. In the direction You'l find it, with all necessary circumstance To meet with him If you please To make it then a perfect act of Noblenesse, You may take notice, that I long have loved him, And if you finde him cold, in the perusall: Tell him I had the promise of his faith, When I gave up my heart, i'th presence of A thousand Angels, that will witnesse it: If yet hee bee not soft to stirre up his Compassion, tell him how I live, and languish, You may report you saw mee weepe, I have not Much more to say, if you will doe this favour, Twill be an argument of your respect, I see your resolution cooles already. I shall desire to see him agen, my heart Is light upon sudden, please you Vncle Ile in, and play a lesson o'my Lute. Exit. Has truth forsooke mankind? or is it my Fate onely to converse with those that are So cruell and neglectfull of our sexe? Vnhappy Maid is he not yet return'd? Then I despaire to see him: And when I thinke indeed of the imployment, That 'tis against himselfe, I may with justice Accuse my want of judgement, to expect He should performe so hard an imposition: I would I could not thinke of any man, They rob me of my peace: I prethee try Thy voyce, to put my heart in better tune; There is a power in harmony, some say, To charme the unruly motions of the braine: Love is itselfe a melancholy madnesse: Why should not Musicke cure the wound of love? Melancholy hence, goe get Some piece of earth to be thy seat, Here the ayre and nimble fire, Would shoot up to meet desire: Sullen humour, leave her blood, Mix not with the purer floud, But let pleasures swelling there, Make a Spring-tide all the yeere. As well As this restraint will give me leave, and yet It does appeare a part of my enlargement To have your company: I hope your sister Enjoyes her health. Nothing as yet. But I have met occasion to convey A Letter to him, yet I cannot promise: But here's the messenger. The same, I did conceale him for his shame. You are welcome, Sir. Shall I beleeve you have beene faithful to My griefes request? Pronounce those words agen. He did say so: What meant she To mocke me with another sad relation? Was't a device in her to increase my joy At meeting, he did talke of comfort; is it A thing restor'd in nature? Oh, before You blesse my eare agen with that wished sound, Excuse my modesty, if my heart present A kisse to thanke you. Now let your comforts flow. Can this be possible? Let me but live to see him, and I write My ambition satisfied Where? Indeed I love him still and shall doe ever, Nor had I now returnd to life, but that I had not tooke my leave of him If you'l oblige a Virgin, For ever to you once more visit him, Tell him I lye like one thats desperate sicke, Opprest with griefe of body, and of mind, But cannot be so fortunate to quit The world till he vouchsafe to visit me. Bid him not feare I will detaine him long ▪ With idle talke, sixe words and I am dead. Although he love me not, he may doe this: If you will adde this to your other worke, I will impose no more, indeed I will not: So farewell noble Sir. Exit. MAy I beleeve my selfe so fortunate? Art thou return'd, or doe I dreame thus happily? Are these my Thornays armes? are those his lips? Can hee repent his cruelty and love? How soone are all my teares dryed up? I doe Forgive my griefes, and thinke they have been modest, And gentle sufferings, who can merit such A joy, that has not felt a world of sorrow? Let us imbrace agen, and if thou canst Confirme mee yet more, that I am awake, And taste my true delight. We are betraid. I hope my breath has not offen ded you. Pray stay a little. Oh let me flie into his armes and boast Never had woman such a noble servant, Blest was that minute Vncle, in which you First knew this Gentleman; more blessed I, That doe enjoy by him, that which my heart Next heaven affecteth most; 'twill be an age Till holy Church confirmes our vowes, I cannot ▪ Mannage the comforts you have given mee, I did not thinke I should so soone have met A husband, Vncle. Noble Sir, what service can reward this goodnesse in you? From Mistresse Chrysolina ? Let me entreate you Sir, peruse that paper. Sir you know Chrysolina ? Poore Gentlewoman is in love with Yongrave : Wee have arriv'd at our desires already, And want but the Church sealing, she is lost, Vnlesse he meet her wishes, 'twill become Our piety to advance, in what wee may The common cause of love, then briefely thus— As you are charitable, goe presently. We'l get off ▪ well enough: Eug. and Thor. whisper. Pray her to meete us. Then I resigne to her, in this alone, I will deserve these noble offices. You know the place. Love her, and let us all be happy. Though I could wish your presence. He ha's prevented us. Exeunt. Sir: if you will acknowledge your Neece. You must accept a Nephew too: we are as fast as they.

Tell me no tellings: Either resigne her to me againe, or— Enough; I am bound to honour thee, command my life, Thou excellent young man. So now tis done; I would not Be engag'd to kisse you againe, for all the estate. Your father left you. I cannot tell, I ha' not kist a woman this twelve-moneth, and had not done this, but that he had my oath to performe it; well you have the lip labour he sent you, Master Yongrave is well, will see you agen shortly—Godbe-wi'y'. You'l send him such another token; imploy your waiting woman, I am no common kisse-carrier. And I be not, I am going Sir, to the place from whence I came Sir? How's that? he go? we must prevent that mischiefe. What doe y' thinke? if ▪ Tis gone againe, wee must have some tricke, To get off without him. Hum? this entertainment is a little better Than I expected. doe y' heare, you may returne, and tell this story Vnto the Lady i'th inchanted Castle: You see my fate, I cannot come; Godbe-wi'yi'. Will you heare him? Doe y' heare; this Lady Is weary of your company; you have Not us'd me like a Gentleman, indeed Scurvily, tis no time nor place to expostulate, But wee shall meet agen; in the meane time, Returne, and tell the Virgin you so magnifie, I doe not finde my selfe in any humour To see her agen; pray her neglect no fortune, For my sake, there be many yonger brothers I'th Towne, will bee content to marry her: You may resolve her what's become of me, There is no wrastling with our fate. Ex. Au. I am ignorant With what words I should meet this noble love. Yes Sir. Mine? excuse me if I suspect. I have heard you Sir. And have considered all that you have said To make me thinke you are now wholly mine: I must confesse you have exprest a Lover, Wanted no Art to flourish your warme passion: But language is no clew to guide us to The knowledge of your heart. It is not; but where circumstances meet, They may be thought on. You lov'd my Sister. And you declare you can neglect her now, Looke on her like a stranger. She lov'd you well, most nobly, with as much Fervour as ever I did or can love; Should I thinke to be more secure than she? Promise that firme to me, which in so fresh A sight and memory you have violated To her, that plac'd you in as deare a bosome? Discretion bids me pause, I may be rash, Either you lov'd her not at all, and so You may play false with both, or loving her With as much levity, I suppose you may Forsake me too. Therfore I bid you first farewell. Exit. Tis granted; But his neglect of you afflicted me. Nor make me blest, while you Seem'd discontented. Best? He is mine. Tis more than will become you sister. And it must bring your modesty in question, To follow one that cares not for you Not while I may challeng interest; here are company Let us withdraw, I have something more to tell you. What did you meane? that Ring was his. Indeed? Then I must tell you Sir, you have not us'd us civilly, to make our conversation ridiculous, To talke and complement with a Boy. Doey' not thinke your wit found out a precious device to make me love you by a president; is this your great Lady? Not now, I know you have art enough to excuse it, Yet I am not mercilesse, let mee entreate Your absence, without ceremony, when You come agen, your talke will bee more musicall. Not so. Alas poore sister, now I feare you not, I see your purpose was to make mee kinde: I wo'd hee were my brother, but let's in And joyne our heads, some counsell would doe well, Tis pitty wee two should leade Apes in hell. Yes, marriage is an act, That doth concerne his whole life, and in something May marre, or profit his eternity: Perhaps the Gentlewoman, since hee gave His faith is falne from vertue. Wee doe not Sir accuse her. This Gentleman pleades for her. Dismisse him first. Ile not question Sir, this Gentlemans relation. But in my confidence, hee hath spoke all truth: I must desire you visit mee no more. Ingratefull man! how are poore women coozen'd? With what impudence couldst thou desire my favour? Goe and make a satisfaction to the injur'd Maid, Borne the dishonour of a man. Exit. That Gentleman? I know the man you love then, is't not Thornay? Why hee's a zealous suiter for my love. If this can be, Thou art the noblest lover in the world, With what affection shall shee be blest That loves him, when the mistresse that esteemes Him not, is thus rewarded? If you will please to joyne with me, I doubt not To effect her wishes. You doe not know what power I have with him. Ile undertake— What reward? I doe admire and love this noble temper, What flames are these? Suppresse 'em, they grow high, If he affect her so, what hope have I? Ex. It was not kindly done, beleeve me sister, He did performe but our request. He could not make you happy, and remaine Servant to me. Doe not thinke I was, I did but carry trouble in my face, When he declared himselfe withdrew my smiles, For your sake, to make you appeare most lovely, And worthy of his choice; and could you be So cruell to reject him, when he came To be confirm'd your owne without a rivall? It seemes he did not know who lov'd him best. Yes, and I in this, will mak't appeare, That now you have exild him from your love, Ile sue for his affection. But you Aurelia are not his; I will Appeale to his modest reason, that shall guide His eye to looke on both agen, I doe not See what in me should not invite him hither, With as much ardor, rather more, since he Hath prov'd already your too much unkindnesse; What if this noble Gentleman should lose His wits upon 't, will all your beautie call His straggling senses to their seate agen? Ile seeke him out betimes and comfort him. How? Thus I may awake his noble flame, nor is it Any dishonor when the world shall know How you have us'd him, if I make returne, To what I lov'd so deerely. Deferre it rather now; here comes my hope. I see no cause. Hee's turnd Ieronymo. Doe y' know where you are? Doe y' pay so much for every kisse? a Diamond? Then hee's gone to her Let other Virgins when they heare this story Wonder, but give mee leave to love you for it, Indeed I doe; looke not so strange, your vertue Compels mee to reaveale it, tis no shame To owne a passion, kindled by such goodnesse. Shee is satisfied, and you are disingaged. I will retire to blush and weepe. Can I be so happy? This truth? Was this the cause? Ile tell Aurelia this. She meant to visit him, but this wil give her wings. I feele Another soule, what raptures are distill'd Vpon my heart? Enter Caperwit. Have I not beene tedious? I told my sister all, and she is gone To Mr. Gerard, if their meeting prosper, I have directed where to find us. But I must aske your blessing, we are married,
Where's this Footman? Goe pray my Vncle Sir Walter Cormorant To dine with me to morrow— And doe y'heare? Tis in your way to aske if my Cosin Bulfinch, The Steward of my Land, bee come to Towne, Hee lies in Fleetstreet betweene Hawke and Buzzard. I'th afternoone, remember Sirrah, that You goe to Master Kite, that lives i'th Poultry, And say I shall expect the thousand pound, Was lent him upon morgage: Sir, beseech your Noblenesse excuse mee, The affaires so neerely doe concerne mee, with A Gentleman, (now your guest,) that I presumed It should not bee offence, if I tooke hold Of this occasion, to speake with him. By no meanes Let me appeare so troublesome, your presence Will be no hurt to my designe, you shall Command a great deale more. That's my feare indeed; For who can looke with eyes like mine upon you, And not be tempted to the same desires? But be not Sir deceived, all forheads are not True glasses of the minde, and beauty alone Deserves not such a blessing ▪ young men doe Too hastily betray themselves to miserie, That thinke no heaven but in their Mistresse face, Looke on my fortune, which doth spread more riches, Than pleasure can instruct thee wayes to spend, Delights shall streame themselves into thy bosome, Honour and titles of the state shall woe Thy name to put them on and not be thine But thou their ornament. I may suspect I have offended these; But pray interpret fairely, noble Sir, to Simple. I doe beseech you pardon The errors that you finde in us fraile women, Yet I beleeve you would not use me so Neglectfully: tis time, I take my leave. I leave you to repent Your cruelty, my Coach— You have strangely wonne me to obey you Sir, I refuse nothing you command. No matter. I did not thinke to have returnd so soone A trouble to you but the importunity Of this most worthy Gentleman prevail'd, I thinke there was some Magick in his tongue. He did no sooner open his desires, But he did wound my heart, you see his bounty, What jewels hee has given mee. I must confesse, I lov'd another lately, but his affection's frozen up— Sir, you are come most seasonably, before These Gentlewomen, I release your promise, My thoughts are fixt upon this Noble Knight, Affect now where you please; here is my husband. There is no way but to acknowledge it, It is no shame in love, there's no disgrace, For else by Law he may recover mee. Be wise and let him have it, 'tis like his within my Cabi net, let's be quit on him, ▪ this will secure our marriage. I will obey you Sir.
Sir, after all, let me obtaine your priviledge. I shall accuse my selfe of too much boldnesse, If you neglect mee Sir before all these; I come not to disturbe you, nor to publish What you have taken from mee. But Sir, you might have been so kind, to have seene your friend once in three dayes. Among them all, there is not one That more desires your happinesse. Y'are modest, And thus increase your value. My blushes speake me guilty, and I feare Betray my frailty to these Gentlewomen: You'l sinne against your knowledge Sir, to make A question how much I esteeme you, be not A tyrant, if my opinion of your worth Prevaile against my modesty, to say I cannot choose but love you, tis my fate, My breeding never suffred, but in this, That I should lose my selfe to court a man, Ambitious of my favour; tis in vaine To tell you, with what art, my eyes have beene Courted by great ones for their smile, for you Will turne them all to teares.
How does my deare Eugenia? And more felicity Than I can boast mine owne, shee's halfe a Bride. Happy ith' embraces of her wished servant; You know our story; he ha's chosen her, And most uncivilly neglecteth me. Thus laden with his scorne, I come to practise A scene of sorrow w'ye; sure thy fate Hath spun a thread for me, we are so like In our misfortunes: Have you heard no newe ▪ Of your ingratefull servant, for I know No other name, and he indeed deserves To have no other memory ▪ that takes A pride in his disdaine. Never to me: or if you had this newes Is recompence enough.
Here, In me your truest servant is return'd. Then I must tell you. Heaven do's heare all this. Her vncle (Whose aime is onely profit) hath concluded With me a price for her, and therefore gives Accesse to none, till I ha' prov'd my fortune; But I finde her devoted to you onely, And have conform'd my wishes unto hers; She loves you best, and I preferre you too, Returne, and be her husband, Ile direct you.
